historical_record.description: The western half of the Williams-Polk double house by Polk & Polk, built for the painter Dora Norton Williams, who paid Willis Polk's family for it with half the building and lot.

Laura Ingalls Wilder stayed here with her daughter, the Bulletin reporter Rose Wilder Lane, during the Panama-Pacific Exposition, and wrote home about the flat and its view of the bay in the letters later published as West From Home.

The Board of Permit Appeals overruled the Department of Public Works' denial of a permit to alter the building at 1019 Vallejo Street in further hearing, with stipulations that a fire escape meeting the department's requirements be provided on the west side of the building, including steps to provide access to windows opening onto fire escape balconies, and that the basement storage area be either sprinklered or cleared of stored items.
The Board of Permit Appeals upheld the Department of Public Works and denied the permit to alter the building at 1019 Vallejo Street, two votes to overrule falling short of the four required.

building.completed_conflict: Recorded as built 1892; the assessor's roll gives 1900.

notable_residents.name: Dora Norton Williams
notable_residents.detail: The painter Dora Norton Williams (1829–1915), widow of Virgil Williams and a close friend of Robert Louis Stevenson and Fanny Osbourne, lived here from 1892 until about 1908.

notable_residents.name: Edward L. Holmes
notable_residents.detail: The architect Edward L. Holmes, partner of the later City Architect Newton J. Tharp, rented here from 1900 to 1904.

notable_residents.name: Rose Wilder Lane
notable_residents.detail: Rose Wilder Lane, then a reporter for the San Francisco Bulletin, rented here about 1915–1916; her mother Laura Ingalls Wilder stayed with her during the 1915 Exposition, and wrote home about the flat in the letters later published as West From Home.
